learningObjectives.title: 9.3 Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability

questions.q: The graph shows the potential energy of a pair of H atoms as a function of the distance between their nuclei. Points V, W, X, and Z are marked on the curve. Which point represents the two atoms separated by the equilibrium bond length of H₂?
options: Point V
Point W
Point X
Point Z
optionWhy: A student who thinks bonded atoms sit as close together as possible picks this. At V the nuclei are so close that their repulsion gives the pair a higher potential energy than the separated atoms have; the pair is not at its most stable separation.

The equilibrium bond length is the separation at which the potential energy of the pair is lowest. W is the minimum of the curve, at about 74 pm: at shorter distances repulsion between the nuclei raises the energy, and at longer distances the attraction is weaker.

A student who thinks the bond length is where the potential energy is zero picks this. At X the pair has the same potential energy as the separated atoms; the minimum, at W, lies at a larger separation.

A student who thinks atoms are bonded as soon as they begin to attract picks this. At Z the attraction is weak and the energy is only slightly below zero; the atoms are held most stably at the minimum, W.
questions.explain: The equilibrium bond length is the separation at which the potential energy of the pair is lowest. W is the minimum of the curve, at about 74 pm: at shorter distances repulsion between the nuclei raises the energy, and at longer distances the attraction is weaker.

figure.alt: Graph of Potential energy (kJ/mol), axis marked −500, −400, −300, −200, −100, 0, 100, 200 and 300, with a line at 0, against Distance between nuclei (pm), axis marked 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300. One curve falls steeply from high energy at very short distance, crosses 0 near 39 pm, reaches a minimum of about −436 kJ/mol at about 74 pm, then rises gradually toward 0 at large distance. Marked points: V on the steep part at about 34 pm and +200 kJ/mol; X where the curve crosses 0; W at the minimum; Z at about 260 pm and −21 kJ/mol.

questions.q: On a graph of potential energy versus internuclear distance for two atoms that form a diatomic molecule, which quantity is the bond energy of the molecule?
options: The increase in potential energy from the curve's lowest point to complete separation
The value of the potential energy at the minimum, including its negative sign
The energy released as the atoms move from the minimum to a large separation
The value of the potential energy when the two atoms are very far apart
optionWhy: The bond energy is the energy required to separate the atoms: the increase in potential energy from the bottom of the curve (the minimum) to the energy of the atoms far apart. It is a positive quantity, equal to the depth of the minimum below the energy of the separated atoms.

A student who copies the coordinate of the minimum as the bond energy picks this. The bond energy is the energy that must be absorbed, a positive amount equal to the depth of the minimum below the energy of the separated atoms.
A student who thinks breaking a bond releases stored energy picks this. Moving from the minimum to large separation raises the potential energy, so energy is absorbed, not released.

A student who takes the value at one point for the change between two points picks this. The potential energy of separated atoms is the reference level (usually 0); the bond energy is the difference between it and the minimum.
questions.explain: The bond energy is the energy required to separate the atoms: the increase in potential energy from the bottom of the curve (the minimum) to the energy of the atoms far apart. It is a positive quantity, equal to the depth of the minimum below the energy of the separated atoms.
questions.working: Bond energy = energy required to separate the bonded atoms = (potential energy of the separated atoms) − (potential energy at the minimum). With the separated atoms at 0, this is the depth of the minimum, a positive quantity.

questions.q: The reaction energy profile shown is for a hypothetical elementary reaction. Which numbered arrow represents the activation energy for the forward reaction?
options: Arrow 1
Arrow 2
Arrow 3
Arrow 4
optionWhy: The activation energy for the forward reaction is the energy difference between the reactants and the transition state, so it is the arrow from the reactant level up to the peak.

A student who thinks that the activation energy is the energy difference between reactants and products picks this arrow. That arrow shows the overall energy change; Eₐ is measured from the reactants up to the transition state.

A student who thinks that the activation energy is the energy of the transition state read from the axis picks this arrow. Eₐ is a difference: the energy of the transition state minus the energy of the reactants, not the whole height of the peak.

A student who thinks that the activation energy is the energy the reactants already have picks this arrow. That arrow shows the energy of the reactants; Eₐ is the further rise needed to reach the transition state.
questions.explain: The activation energy for the forward reaction is the energy difference between the reactants and the transition state, so it is the arrow from the reactant level up to the peak.

questions.q: A reaction energy profile for an elementary reaction plots energy against the reaction coordinate. What does the reaction coordinate represent?
options: The time that has passed since the reactants were first mixed together
The fraction of the reactant molecules in the sample that have become products
The progress of the atoms' rearrangement from the reactants into the products
The distance that the reactant particles travel before they collide
optionWhy: A student who thinks the horizontal axis is time picks this. The reaction coordinate follows the rearrangement of atoms in one event; a profile says nothing about how long the reaction takes.
A student who reads the profile as a description of the whole sample picks this. The profile describes one elementary reaction event, not how much of a sample has reacted.
The reaction coordinate is the axis along which the complex set of motions that rearranges the reactants into products is plotted: it follows how far one rearrangement has gone.
A student who reads 'coordinate' as a position in space picks this. The reaction coordinate is not a distance traveled; it stands for the progress of the rearrangement of the atoms.
questions.explain: The reaction coordinate is the axis along which the complex set of motions that rearranges the reactants into products is plotted: it follows how far one rearrangement has gone.

questions.q: Which of the following processes is endothermic for the substance that changes?
options: Liquid water evaporating from the surface of wet skin
Molten candle wax becoming solid in a cool mold
Warm water cooling down inside a refrigerator
Steam condensing on the surface of a cold window
optionWhy: Evaporating separates water molecules that attract each other, which requires energy, so the water absorbs energy from the skin; that is why the skin cools.
A student who thinks forming attractions requires energy picks this. As the wax solidifies, attractions between its molecules form and energy is released, so solidifying is exothermic.
A student who thinks the refrigerator puts cold into the water picks this. The water cools because energy is transferred out of it, so for the water the process is exothermic.

A student who judges the process by the cold window rather than by the steam picks this. As steam condenses, attractions form between water molecules and energy is released to the window, so condensing is exothermic.
questions.explain: Evaporating separates water molecules that attract each other, which requires energy, so the water absorbs energy from the skin; that is why the skin cools.

questions.q: A sample of liquid water at 0 °C is placed in a freezer. While the water freezes, its temperature stays at 0 °C. How does the energy of the water change while it freezes?
options: It decreases, because energy is transferred from the water to the colder freezer
It stays the same, because the temperature of the water does not change
It increases, because energy is needed to form the attractions that hold the ice together
It decreases, because part of the water's energy is destroyed as the ice forms
optionWhy: Freezing is exothermic: as the molecules settle into the solid and attractions form, energy is released and transferred to the colder surroundings. The temperature stays constant, but the energy of the water decreases.
A student who equates heat with temperature picks this. During a phase change the temperature stays constant while energy is transferred; freezing water releases energy to the freezer.
A student who thinks forming attractions requires energy picks this. Forming attractions between water molecules releases energy, which is why freezing is exothermic.
A student who thinks energy can be destroyed picks this. The energy of the water does decrease, but the energy is transferred to the freezer, not destroyed.
questions.explain: Freezing is exothermic: as the molecules settle into the solid and attractions form, energy is released and transferred to the colder surroundings. The temperature stays constant, but the energy of the water decreases.

questions.q: An energy diagram for a process shows the final state at a higher energy than the initial state. Which process could the diagram represent?
options: Steam condensing to form liquid water on a cold mirror
A candle burning after being lit with a match
Ice melting to form liquid water on a warm day
Iron rusting inside a hand warmer as it gets hot
optionWhy: A student who thinks forming attractions requires energy picks this. As steam condenses, attractions form between water molecules and energy is released, so the liquid is lower in energy than the steam.

A student who thinks a reaction that needs a flame to start is endothermic picks this. The match supplies only the activation energy; burning wax releases energy, so its products are lower in energy than the reactants.
Melting separates water molecules that attract one another in the solid, which requires energy; the liquid is higher in energy than the ice, so melting is endothermic.

A student who thinks a process that heats its surroundings has gained energy picks this. The hand warmer gets hot because the rusting iron transfers energy to it, so the products are lower in energy than the reactants.
questions.explain: Melting separates water molecules that attract one another in the solid, which requires energy; the liquid is higher in energy than the ice, so melting is endothermic.

questions.q: An energy diagram for a hypothetical reaction shows the reactants at 50 kJ/mol, a single maximum at 110 kJ/mol and the products at 20 kJ/mol. What is the energy change for the reaction?
options: −30 kJ/mol
+30 kJ/mol
+60 kJ/mol
−90 kJ/mol
optionWhy: The energy change is the energy of the products minus that of the reactants: 20 − 50 = −30 kJ/mol. The products are lower in energy, so the reaction is exothermic and the change is negative.
A student who writes energy that is released as a positive change picks this. The system ends 30 kJ/mol lower in energy, so its energy change is −30 kJ/mol.
A student who reads the rise to the maximum as the energy change picks this: 110 − 50 = 60 kJ/mol. That rise is the activation energy; the energy change compares the products with the reactants.

A student who takes the energy change as the drop from the maximum to the products picks this: 20 − 110 = −90 kJ/mol. Part of that drop only returns the 60 kJ/mol absorbed on the way up; the net change is 20 − 50 = −30 kJ/mol.
questions.explain: The energy change is the energy of the products minus that of the reactants: 20 − 50 = −30 kJ/mol. The products are lower in energy, so the reaction is exothermic and the change is negative.
questions.working: Energy change = E(products) − E(reactants) = 20 kJ/mol − 50 kJ/mol = −30 kJ/mol (exothermic: the products are lower). Distractors: sign reversed for energy released, +30 kJ/mol; rise to the peak, 110 − 50 = +60 kJ/mol; drop from the peak to the products, 20 − 110 = −90 kJ/mol.

questions.q: A hot piece of copper is placed in cool water in an insulated cup, and the water becomes warmer. Which statement best describes, at the particulate level, how the water is warmed?
options: Heat, a substance held between the copper atoms, flows out of the metal and spreads among the water molecules
Cold leaves the water molecules and passes into the copper, so the water molecules are left warmer than before
Copper atoms collide with water molecules, which leave the collisions with more kinetic energy on average
Copper atoms pass on their high temperature to the water molecules, so each molecule becomes hot in itself
optionWhy: A student who thinks heat is a substance stored in hot objects picks this. Nothing material passes from the copper to the water; energy is transferred in collisions and appears as faster motion of the water molecules.
A student who thinks cold is something that moves out of cold objects picks this. Cold is not a substance or a form of energy; the water warms because energy is transferred to it from the copper.

The atoms of the hot copper have a greater average kinetic energy than the water molecules. In collisions at the surface of the metal, energy is transferred on average from the copper atoms to the water molecules, whose average kinetic energy, and so the water's temperature, rises.

A student who thinks each particle of a hot object is itself hot picks this. A single atom or molecule has kinetic energy, not a temperature; what is passed on in collisions is kinetic energy, and temperature describes the average for the whole sample.
questions.explain: The atoms of the hot copper have a greater average kinetic energy than the water molecules. In collisions at the surface of the metal, energy is transferred on average from the copper atoms to the water molecules, whose average kinetic energy, and so the water's temperature, rises.

questions.q: Two solid blocks, each at a uniform temperature, are pressed together inside an insulated box. Which information is sufficient to predict the direction of the net transfer of energy as heat between the blocks?
options: The total thermal energy of each block
The mass and size of each of the blocks
The material each block is made from
The temperature of each of the blocks
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is transferred from the body with more energy in total picks this. A large cool block can hold more energy in total than a small hot one, yet the net transfer is from the hot block to the cool one.

A student who thinks a bigger or heavier object is the hotter one, and so gives out energy, picks this. Size does not fix the temperature: the net transfer is from whichever block is at the higher temperature.

A student who thinks each material has its own natural temperature, with metals being cold, picks this. Any material can be at any temperature; the direction depends on which block is warmer, not on what the blocks are made of.

The warmer block is the one whose particles have the greater average kinetic energy, and collisions transfer energy on balance from that block to the cooler one. Knowing the two temperatures is therefore enough to give the direction.
questions.explain: The warmer block is the one whose particles have the greater average kinetic energy, and collisions transfer energy on balance from that block to the cooler one. Knowing the two temperatures is therefore enough to give the direction.
questions.working: No calculation. Collisions transfer energy, on balance, from the body whose particles have the greater average kinetic energy to the body whose particles have the lower average kinetic energy. The average kinetic energy of the particles is indicated by the temperature, so the two temperatures are sufficient: the net transfer is from the block at the higher temperature to the block at the lower temperature. Total energy, size and material do not fix the direction.

questions.q: A 50.0 g block of copper at 80.0°C is placed in contact with a 200.0 g block of aluminum at 30.0°C inside an insulated box. Which statement describes the energy transfer that occurs?
options: Energy is transferred from the aluminum to the copper until both contain equal thermal energy
Cold is transferred from the aluminum to the copper until their temperatures are equal
Energy is transferred from the copper to the aluminum until their temperatures are equal
Energy is transferred from the copper to the aluminum until both hold equal thermal energy
optionWhy: A student who thinks heat flows from the object containing more thermal energy, here the larger aluminum block, to the one containing less picks this. The direction is set by temperature: the copper is hotter, so energy flows from the copper to the aluminum, and it stops when the temperatures are equal.
A student who thinks cold flows from a cold object into a warm one picks this. Cold is not transferred; the copper cools because it loses energy to the aluminum.

Heat flows from the body at the higher temperature to the body at the lower temperature. Collisions at the contact surface transfer energy from the copper to the aluminum until the particles in both blocks have the same average kinetic energy, that is, until their temperatures are equal.

A student who thinks thermal equilibrium means equal amounts of thermal energy picks this. Transfer stops when the temperatures are equal; at that point the larger aluminum block holds more total thermal energy than the copper.
questions.explain: Heat flows from the body at the higher temperature to the body at the lower temperature. Collisions at the contact surface transfer energy from the copper to the aluminum until the particles in both blocks have the same average kinetic energy, that is, until their temperatures are equal.

questions.q: The box labeled Before represents a sample of N₂(g) in a sealed, rigid container at 25°C. The line behind each molecule indicates its speed; a longer line means a faster molecule. The sample is heated to 75°C. Which of the numbered diagrams best represents the sample at 75°C?
options: Diagram 1
Diagram 2
Diagram 3
Diagram 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks particles expand when heated picks this. The molecules themselves do not change size; heating makes them move faster, which this diagram does not show.
A student who thinks heated gas particles rise to the top of a container picks this. In a sealed container heated evenly, the molecules stay spread through the whole volume and move faster.
A student who thinks heating breaks molecules into atoms picks this. Heating N₂ from 25°C to 75°C makes the molecules move faster; it does not break the bond between the two N atoms.
Heating the gas increases its energy: the molecules move faster on average, shown by the longer lines. The molecules keep their size and identity and stay spread through the whole container.
questions.explain: Heating the gas increases its energy: the molecules move faster on average, shown by the longer lines. The molecules keep their size and identity and stay spread through the whole container.

questions.q: The heating curve shown is for a sample of water heated at a constant rate, starting as ice at −40°C. Which statement describes what happens during segment BC?
options: No energy is absorbed, which is why the temperature of the sample stays constant
Energy is absorbed as O–H bonds within the molecules break, while the temperature stays constant
Energy is released as molecules leave the solid's structure, while the temperature stays constant
Energy is absorbed as the solid's structure breaks down, while the temperature stays constant
optionWhy: A student who thinks a substance absorbing energy must rise in temperature picks this. The heater keeps supplying energy during BC; the ice absorbs it as it melts, at constant temperature.
A student who thinks melting breaks covalent bonds within molecules picks this. Melting overcomes attractions between water molecules; the O–H bonds stay intact, and liquid water is still H₂O.
A student who thinks breaking the attractions that hold particles together releases energy picks this. Separating attracting molecules requires energy, so melting absorbs energy.

Segment BC is the flat segment at 0°C, where ice melts. Energy from the heater is absorbed to overcome attractions between the water molecules in the solid, so the system's energy increases while its temperature stays at the melting point.
questions.explain: Segment BC is the flat segment at 0°C, where ice melts. Energy from the heater is absorbed to overcome attractions between the water molecules in the solid, so the system's energy increases while its temperature stays at the melting point.

questions.q: The molar enthalpy of vaporization of water at 100°C is 40.7 kJ/mol. How much energy is released when 1.60 g of steam at 100°C condenses to liquid water at 100°C?
optionWhy: A student who multiplies a molar enthalpy by a mass in grams picks this: (1.60)(40.7) = 65.1. The value is per mole, so the mass must first be converted to moles.
n = 1.60 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.0888 mol. Condensing releases the same energy per mole that vaporizing absorbs, so the energy released is (0.0888 mol)(40.7 kJ/mol) = 3.61 kJ.
A student who thinks the molar enthalpy is the energy for the whole sample picks this. 40.7 kJ is released per mole; this sample is only 0.0888 mol.
A student who applies q = mcΔT to the phase change picks this: with ΔT = 0, q = 0. Condensation releases energy at constant temperature, found from n × ΔH.
questions.explain: n = 1.60 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.0888 mol. Condensing releases the same energy per mole that vaporizing absorbs, so the energy released is (0.0888 mol)(40.7 kJ/mol) = 3.61 kJ.
questions.working: n = 1.60 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.0888 mol. Condensation is the reverse of vaporization: molar enthalpy of condensation = −40.7 kJ/mol, so the energy released = (0.0888 mol)(40.7 kJ/mol) = 3.61 kJ.

questions.q: When aqueous solutions of an acid and a base are mixed, an exothermic reaction occurs and the temperature of the solution rises. Which statement best explains the rise in temperature at the particle level?
options: Breaking the bonds in the reactants releases the energy stored in them, which makes all of the particles move faster
The products have lower potential energy than the reactants, and the difference becomes kinetic energy
The products have higher potential energy than the reactants, and that extra energy is what makes the solution hotter
The reaction produces particles of heat, which spread out among the water molecules and raise the solution's temperature
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is stored in bonds and released when they break picks this. Breaking bonds requires energy; the energy comes out when the new bonds in the products form.

Bonds broken and formed in the reaction leave the products with less chemical potential energy than the reactants. The energy difference increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, which is measured as a higher temperature.

A student who thinks more chemical potential energy means a higher temperature picks this. If the products had more potential energy, that energy would come from the particles' kinetic energy and the solution would cool.
A student who thinks heat is made of particles picks this. The energy released makes the existing particles move faster; no particles of heat are produced.
questions.explain: Bonds broken and formed in the reaction leave the products with less chemical potential energy than the reactants. The energy difference increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, which is measured as a higher temperature.

questions.q: Hydrogen and fluorine react exothermically: H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2 HF(g). The reaction can be thought of as taking place in two stages: the bonds in the reactant molecules break, and then the bonds in the product molecules form. Which statement correctly describes the potential energy of the system during these stages?
options: It falls as the H–H and F–F bonds break and rises as the H–F bonds form
It rises as the H–H and F–F bonds break and rises as the H–F bonds form
It rises as the H–H and F–F bonds break and falls as the H–F bonds form
It falls as the H–H and F–F bonds break and falls as the H–F bonds form
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is stored in bonds and released when they break picks this. Breaking bonds requires energy and raises the potential energy; forming bonds releases energy and lowers it.
A student who thinks making bonds, like breaking them, needs an input of energy picks this. Bond formation releases energy, so the potential energy falls as the H–F bonds form.

Separating bonded atoms requires energy, so the potential energy of the system rises as the H–H and F–F bonds break. Forming the H–F bonds releases energy, so the potential energy falls, and it falls by more than it rose because the reaction is exothermic.
A student who thinks every stage of an exothermic reaction releases energy picks this. Breaking the H–H and F–F bonds requires energy even though the reaction is exothermic overall.
questions.explain: Separating bonded atoms requires energy, so the potential energy of the system rises as the H–H and F–F bonds break. Forming the H–F bonds releases energy, so the potential energy falls, and it falls by more than it rose because the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: For which of the following equations is the standard enthalpy change, ΔH°, equal to the standard enthalpy of formation of CaO(s)?
options: 2 Ca(s) + O₂(g) → 2 CaO(s)
Ca(s) + ½ O₂(g) → CaO(s)
Ca²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g) → CaO(s)
Ca(OH)₂(s) → CaO(s) + H₂O(g)
optionWhy: A student who thinks every equation must use whole-number coefficients picks this. It forms 2 mol of CaO, so its ΔH° is twice ΔH°_f of CaO(s).

One mole of CaO(s) is formed from its elements in their standard states, calcium metal and oxygen gas, so ΔH° for this equation is ΔH°_f of CaO(s). The fraction ½ is needed to keep exactly one mole of product.

A student who thinks a formation reaction builds the compound from the particles it is made of picks this. The reactants must be the elements in their standard states, Ca(s) and O₂(g), not gaseous ions, which are far higher in energy.

A student who thinks any reaction that produces one mole of a compound is its formation reaction picks this; heating calcium hydroxide does produce CaO(s). The reactant is a compound, not the elements, so ΔH° for this reaction is not ΔH°_f of CaO(s).
questions.explain: One mole of CaO(s) is formed from its elements in their standard states, calcium metal and oxygen gas, so ΔH° for this equation is ΔH°_f of CaO(s). The fraction ½ is needed to keep exactly one mole of product.
questions.working: No calculation. A formation reaction makes exactly 1 mol of the compound from its elements in their standard states: Ca(s) and O₂(g). Balancing with 1 mol CaO requires ½ O₂(g): Ca(s) + ½ O₂(g) → CaO(s).

questions.q: The diagram represents the reaction H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g) as two steps, I and II, at the particulate level. Which of the following correctly describes the enthalpy changes of steps I and II?
options: Step I: ΔH > 0; step II: ΔH < 0
Step I: ΔH < 0; step II: ΔH > 0
Step I: ΔH > 0; step II: ΔH > 0
Step I: ΔH < 0; step II: ΔH < 0
optionWhy: Step I separates the atoms of the H₂ and Cl₂ molecules; breaking bonds requires energy, so ΔH > 0. Step II brings H and Cl atoms together to form H–Cl bonds, which releases energy, so ΔH < 0.

A student who thinks bonds store energy, releasing it when broken and taking it in when formed, picks this. Breaking bonds requires energy and forming bonds releases energy, so the signs are the other way round.
A student who thinks that forming a bond requires an input of energy picks this. Step I is correctly endothermic, but when H and Cl atoms bond in step II energy is released, so ΔH < 0.
A student who thinks breaking bonds releases energy picks this. Step II is correctly exothermic, but separating the atoms in H₂ and Cl₂ in step I requires energy, so ΔH > 0.
questions.explain: Step I separates the atoms of the H₂ and Cl₂ molecules; breaking bonds requires energy, so ΔH > 0. Step II brings H and Cl atoms together to form H–Cl bonds, which releases energy, so ΔH < 0.
questions.working: No calculation. Step I breaks the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, which requires energy (ΔH > 0). Step II forms H–Cl bonds, which releases energy (ΔH < 0).

questions.q: A reference book describes a reaction with ΔG° = −120 kJ/mol_rxn at 298 K as “spontaneous.” Which statement about the reaction at 298 K is best supported by this value of ΔG°?
options: It is thermodynamically favored under standard conditions
Once its reactants are mixed, it occurs very rapidly
It begins by itself, without needing any input of energy to start
It gives off 120 kJ of heat for each mole of reaction
optionWhy: ΔG° < 0 means the reaction is thermodynamically favored under standard conditions. That is all the sign of ΔG° shows; it says nothing about how fast the reaction is, whether it needs energy to start, or how much heat it releases.
A student who reads 'spontaneous' as 'quick or sudden' picks this. ΔG° says whether a reaction is favored, not how fast it goes; a favored reaction can be extremely slow.
A student who reads 'spontaneous' as 'happening without cause' picks this. Many favored reactions need a spark or heating to begin; ΔG° < 0 does not rule that out.
A student who treats ΔG° as the heat of reaction picks this. The heat released at constant pressure is given by ΔH°, which differs from ΔG° by the −TΔS° term.
questions.explain: ΔG° < 0 means the reaction is thermodynamically favored under standard conditions. That is all the sign of ΔG° shows; it says nothing about how fast the reaction is, whether it needs energy to start, or how much heat it releases.

questions.q: The numbered diagrams are possible representations of one cation and one anion of the soluble ionic solid MX, with nearby water molecules, after MX has dissolved in water. In each water molecule, the larger circle represents the O atom. Which diagram best represents the interaction of the dissolved ions with the solvent?
options: Diagram 1
Diagram 2
Diagram 3
Diagram 4
optionWhy: Dissolved ions are separated from one another, and each is surrounded by water molecules held by ion-dipole attractions: the partially negative O atoms of water are nearest the cation M⁺, and the partially positive H atoms are nearest the anion X⁻. This interaction of the dissolved species with the solvent is one of the factors in ΔG° of dissolution.

A student who has the partial charges of water the wrong way round picks the box in which H atoms are nearest M⁺ and O atoms are nearest X⁻. The O atom of water is partially negative and is attracted to the cation; the H atoms are partially positive and are attracted to the anion.

A student who treats water as a passive medium picks the box in which the ions are apart but the water molecules have no particular orientation. Water molecules are polar and are attracted to the ions, so those nearest an ion turn the oppositely charged end toward it.

A student who thinks a dissolved ionic compound remains as intact MX units picks the box in which M⁺ and X⁻ stay in contact. A soluble ionic solid dissolves as separate ions, each with its own surrounding water molecules.
questions.explain: Dissolved ions are separated from one another, and each is surrounded by water molecules held by ion-dipole attractions: the partially negative O atoms of water are nearest the cation M⁺, and the partially positive H atoms are nearest the anion X⁻. This interaction of the dissolved species with the solvent is one of the factors in ΔG° of dissolution.
